Note to Vikas, typed on my phone on the train back

Bhai, I went home this weekend. Papa walked me to the auto stand like always, but he stopped twice to catch his breath, and pretended it was to check his phone. At dinner he asked me to repeat things three times. He used to be the loudest one at every wedding.
I didn't say anything to him. I just walked slower too. On the train I cried a bit, which surprised me.
What I did next: I called Mummy and asked, gently, whether Papa has seen a doctor about his breath and hearing. She said he'd been putting it off. I've booked a check-up for him on the 18th and I'll take leave to go with him. Can you call him this week, just to chat?

Sharmila

qa.a: He stopped twice to catch his breath.

qa.q: What did Sharmila feel on the train back?
qa.a: Sharmila felt a wave of sadness, enough to cry, which came as a surprise.

qa.q: What practical steps did Sharmila take after noticing the changes?
qa.a: Sharmila quietly walked slower with Papa, asked Mummy gently about a doctor, booked a check-up and asked Vikas to call him.

qa.q: Why might Papa have pretended to check his phone when he stopped?
qa.a: He may not want his children to see him slowing down, perhaps to protect his pride or to avoid worrying them.

grounding: It shows an adult child noticing a parent walk slower and hear less, feeling sudden sadness and protectiveness, and quietly acting on it.

passage:
Sunday, 11 pm

Went to Amma's for lunch today with Kishore. Amma had made her fish curry like always, but when Kishore asked for the salt she didn't hear him. He asked again. She laughed and said, "This curry needs no salt!" but I could tell she'd missed it.
Later she sat down halfway through washing up. She never used to sit down in the kitchen. She used to carry me on her hip while stirring two pots.
On the drive home I was quiet. Kishore squeezed my hand. I felt this huge, quiet sadness, and also a fierce wish to wrap her in cotton wool.
I won't do that. She'd hate it. But next Sunday I'll wash up with her, and I'll gently ask if she wants to get her ears checked.

Preeti

qa.q: What had Amma cooked for lunch?
qa.a: Amma had made her fish curry.

qa.q: What did Preeti feel on the drive home?
qa.a: Preeti felt a huge, quiet sadness and a fierce wish to protect Amma.

qa.q: What wise step does Preeti plan for next Sunday?
qa.a: To wash up alongside Amma and gently ask about an ear check, rather than taking over.

qa.q: How might Amma feel if Preeti wrapped her in cotton wool?
qa.a: Amma would probably feel smothered and hurt in her pride, which is why Preeti says she would hate it.

grounding: It shows an adult child noticing a parent hearing less and tiring faster, feeling sadness and protectiveness at this quiet milestone.

passage: Rafiq came home to the village near Malegaon for Eid, twenty-five and full of city stories. On the first morning he went to the fields with Abbu, as he had done since he was a boy. But halfway down the path, Abbu stopped to rest against the neem tree. His breath was short. He waved Rafiq ahead. 'Go on, I'll catch up.' Rafiq's friend Chetan, working in the next field, called out, 'Your Abbu's been resting there every morning this year.' Rafiq looked back at the old man under the tree, the man who used to carry him on his shoulders across these fields. A wave of sadness went through him, and something fierce and protective. He walked back and sat under the neem with Abbu, and they talked about the crops until Abbu was ready.

qa.q: Where did Abbu stop to rest?
qa.a: Against the neem tree.

qa.q: What did Rafiq feel as he looked back at Abbu?
qa.a: He felt a wave of sadness and a fierce protectiveness.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that showed respect?
qa.a: He went back and sat with Abbu under the tree, talking about crops until Abbu was ready, instead of rushing him.

qa.q: How might Abbu have felt when Rafiq came back to sit with him?
qa.a: Abbu may have felt a little embarrassed about slowing down but also touched and comforted.

grounding: Shows an adult child noticing a parent tiring faster and feeling sadness and protectiveness at seeing the ageing of someone who once cared for him.

passage: Oskar, twenty-four, hadn't visited his mother in Gothenburg since spring. When he rang the bell, it took a long time for her to come. Selin opened the door smiling, but she was holding the rail, and when he said hello she said, 'Pardon, darling?' At dinner she asked him to repeat himself four times. After she went to bed early, tired, Oskar sat alone at the kitchen table where she used to help him with homework. He felt a sudden, heavy sadness, and a fierce urge to fix everything at once: stair rails, hearing tests, grocery deliveries. He took a breath. Tomorrow he'd ask her what she wanted. For now, he washed the dishes the way she liked them, glasses first.

qa.q: How many times did Selin ask Oskar to repeat himself?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What did Oskar feel at the kitchen table?
qa.a: He felt a sudden heavy sadness and a strong protective urge to fix everything.

qa.q: Why is Oskar's decision to ask Selin tomorrow wise?
qa.a: It respects her wishes and dignity instead of rushing to change everything without her.

qa.q: How might Selin feel if Oskar asks what she wants?
qa.a: She would likely feel respected and cared for, still in charge of her own life.

passage: In the waiting room of the ear clinic, Vishal watched his father, Imran, lean towards the receptionist and say, "Sorry? Once more?" for the third time. When had Abbu started doing that? Vishal remembered him striding ahead on the beach road, Vishal's small hand in his, calling out the names of ships. Now Abbu walked slowly back from the counter and lowered himself into the plastic chair with a small grunt. Something tightened in Vishal's throat. He wanted to fix it, to shout at time, to carry him. Instead he lifted the heavy file off Abbu's lap and said, "Next time I'll stand at the counter with you, and you tell me what they got wrong." Abbu smiled. "You were always nosy." Their token came up, and they went in together.

qa.q: What did Imran say to the receptionist for the third time?
qa.a: He said, "Sorry? Once more?"

qa.q: What does the tightening in Vishal's throat suggest?
qa.a: Vishal felt a sudden wave of sadness and protectiveness, seeing his once-striding father slow down.

qa.q: How did Vishal handle the moment respectfully?
qa.a: He helped quietly with the file and offered to stand beside Abbu at the counter while keeping Abbu in charge, instead of taking over.

qa.q: How might Imran feel about his son noticing his slowness?
qa.a: He may feel a little exposed, but his joke about Vishal being nosy suggests he feels loved rather than pitied.

grounding: Shows an adult child seeing a parent hear less and move slower, feeling a quiet wave of sadness and protectiveness at this milestone.
